core: Distribution of Earth's water: ~97% saltwater, ~3% freshwater; most freshwater in ice and groundwater
High-level water cycle and the concept of recharge
Water use by sector (US and global); withdrawal vs consumptive use
Groundwater depletion / aquifer overdraft (Ogallala/High Plains, Central Valley)
Conservation/efficiency and virtual water / water footprint
supporting: Water quality: point vs nonpoint source pollution (brief)
outOfScope: Ecosystems and natural-capital framing (owned by Ecosystems and Natural Resources)
In-depth agriculture and food systems (owned by Sustainable Food Systems; only water's role covered here)
Urban water infrastructure systems in depth (owned by Sustainable Cities)

claims.claim: About 96.5% of Earth's water is saltwater in the oceans; roughly 3.5% is freshwater, of which about 68.7% is in glaciers/ice and about 30.1% is groundwater, leaving surface water in rivers and lakes a tiny fraction (rivers ~2,120 km3, about one ten-thousandth of one percent of all water).

The water cycle, driven by solar energy and gravity, moves water through evaporation/transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration/recharge, and runoff, with no beginning or end, making surface water and shallow groundwater renewable within their recharge rate.

US total water withdrawals in 2015 were about 322 Bgal/d (9% below 2010's 354 Bgal/d, lowest since before 1970); the three largest categories were thermoelectric power 133 Bgal/d (41%), irrigation 118 Bgal/d (37%), and public supply 39 Bgal/d (12%), together ~90% of the total.

Withdrawal (water removed from a source) differs from consumptive use (water not returned). Thermoelectric power leads US withdrawals but returns most cooling water; irrigation consumed about 62% (73.2 Bgal/d) of its 2015 withdrawals.
Globally, agriculture accounts for about 69% of freshwater withdrawals, with industry near 19% and municipal use near 12%; agriculture is the dominant user across most regions.

Physical water scarcity (introduced in IWMI's 2007 Comprehensive Assessment) exists where the resource itself cannot meet demand; economic water scarcity exists where water is physically available but infrastructure/investment to access it is lacking (common in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia).

Groundwater overdraft in the High Plains (Ogallala) aquifer (which underlies ~174,000 sq mi across eight states) has depleted roughly 330 km3 of largely non-renewable fossil groundwater; California's Central Valley has lost about 80 km3 since the 1960s; together the two regions account for roughly half of US groundwater depletion since 1900.
Estimated cumulative US groundwater depletion during 1900-2008 totals about 1,000 km3, with the rate reaching almost 25 km3 per year during 2000-2008.

Groundwater is neither fully renewable like solar energy nor non-renewable like a petroleum deposit: recharge replenishes it, but often at much smaller rates than withdrawals, so overdraft can persistently draw down storage.

US water pollution is divided into point sources (discrete Clean Water Act discharges) and nonpoint sources (diffuse runoff carrying fertilizers, pesticides, sediment, salts, bacteria, and nutrients); states report nonpoint source pollution as the leading remaining cause of water-quality problems.

Virtual water (introduced by Tony Allan in the early 1990s; Stockholm Water Prize 2008) is the freshwater embedded in producing a good; the water footprint (developed by Arjen Hoekstra, 2002) measures total green, blue, and grey freshwater used to make what a person/business/nation consumes, with roughly 15,000 liters estimated behind one kilogram of beef.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The '15,000 liters per kilogram of beef' figure is widely cited but contested.
positions: Water Footprint Network global average is ~15,000 L/kg, ~93% green (rain-fed feed) water
Critics note the figure blends green and blue water and varies enormously by production system, so it can overstate pressure on scarce blue-water supplies
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a Water Footprint Network estimate that is mostly green water, with an explicit caveat that local context and water source matter; not stated as a fixed universal cost.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic placeholder text ('a foundational concept... introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, sourced claims about water; all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate definition-of-a-concept framing with substantive hydrology and water-use content.
Added dated, sourced quantitative figures (Earth's water distribution, US 2015 withdrawals, global sector shares, groundwater depletion volumes).
Introduced the withdrawal-vs-consumption distinction, which the draft lacked entirely.
rightsIssues: All sources treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced. USGS, EPA, and FAO content is government/intergovernmental. Water Footprint Network and Global Water Forum are secondary; only facts and definitions used, reworded originally.
The '15,000 L/kg beef' figure is attributed to the Water Footprint Network and flagged as contested.

sourceRecords.title: How Much Water Is There on Earth? (USGS Water Science School)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports the distribution of Earth's water: ~96.54% oceans/saltwater, ~3.46% freshwater; of freshwater ~68.7% ice caps/glaciers/permanent snow and ~30.1% groundwater; rivers ~509 mi3 (2,120 km3), about one ten-thousandth of one percent of all water. U.S. federal work (public domain); figures reworded, no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Water Cycle (USGS Water Science School)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports the high-level water-cycle description: continuous movement among atmosphere, land, and subsurface via evaporation/evapotranspiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration/recharge, runoff/streamflow, and snowmelt; driven by solar energy and gravity; the statement that ~96% of Earth's water is in the oceans and that human activity alters storage, movement, and quality. U.S. federal work; reworded originally.

sourceRecords.title: Summary of Estimated Water Use in the United States in 2015 (USGS Fact Sheet 2018-3035; Circular 1441)
sourceRecords.notes: Fact-sheet summary of USGS Circular 1441. Figures corroborated across the USGS 'Total Water Use' and thermoelectric pages and the Circular 1441 record (downloaded fs20183035.pdf; text layer did not extract, so figures were verified from the USGS web pages and Circular 1441 abstract). Supports: 2015 US total withdrawals 322 Bgal/d, 9% below 2010's 354 Bgal/d and lowest since before 1970; the three largest categories thermoelectric 133 Bgal/d (41%), irrigation 118 Bgal/d (37%), public supply 39 Bgal/d (12%), together ~90% of the national total; and that irrigation consumptive use was about 62% (73.2 Bgal/d) of irrigation withdrawals, with thermoelectric withdrawals nearly all surface water returned to the source. U.S. federal work (public domain); reworded originally.

sourceRecords.title: AQUASTAT — Water withdrawal by sector (methodology / global ratios)
sourceRecords.provider: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19 (followed 301 redirect to the index.html copy). Supports the global freshwater withdrawal ratios of about 69% agricultural, 12% municipal, and 19% industrial, the note that the global figures are weighted by a few high-withdrawal countries, and that the agricultural share ranges from more than 80% in Africa and Asia to just over 20% in Europe. Intergovernmental source; only figures used, reworded originally.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding water scarcity: definitions and measurements (IWMI 2007 physical vs economic scarcity)
sourceRecords.provider: Global Water Forum (summarizing IWMI Comprehensive Assessment of Water Management in Agriculture, 2007)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Secondary source that states the physical-vs-economic water scarcity distinction was defined in IWMI's 2007 Comprehensive Assessment: physical scarcity = the resource itself cannot meet demand (including environmental needs); economic scarcity = water is available but investment/infrastructure to access it is lacking. Corroborated by a WebSearch summary noting economic scarcity predominates in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia. Definitions reworded originally; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Groundwater Depletion in the United States (1900-2008) (USGS SIR 2013-5079, Konikow)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the USGS publication summary page via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: estimated cumulative US groundwater depletion 1900-2008 of approximately 1,000 km3; a 108-year average depletion rate of about 9.2 km3/yr; and an accelerated rate of almost 25 km3/yr during 2000-2008, based on 40 aquifers/areas. Authored by Leonard F. Konikow. U.S. federal work (public domain); figures reworded.

sourceRecords.title: Groundwater depletion and sustainability of irrigation in the US High Plains and Central Valley (Scanlon et al., 2012, PNAS; also a USGS publication)
sourceRecords.provider: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences / U.S. Geological Survey
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract and findings obtained via WebSearch on 2026-08-19 (PNAS full text and USGS pub page 70176442 returned 403 to the fetcher). Supports: focused depletion of ~330 km3 of largely fossil groundwater in the central/southern High Plains (Ogallala), mostly recharged over the past ~13,000 years, with about a third of depletion concentrated in ~4% of the aquifer area; ~80 km3 of Central Valley depletion since the 1960s, concentrated during droughts; and that these two irrigated regions account for roughly 50% of US groundwater depletion since 1900. High Plains extent (~174,000 sq mi, eight states) corroborated by the USGS High Plains Aquifer page. Peer-reviewed; figures used, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is a Water Footprint? / Virtual water and the water footprint concept
sourceRecords.provider: Water Footprint Network (concepts by A. Y. Hoekstra and J. A. Allan)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: the water footprint as a measure of freshwater appropriation across supply chains, developed by Arjen Y. Hoekstra (2002); the green/blue/grey component split; and the estimate of roughly 15,000 liters of water behind one kilogram of beef (about 93% green, 4% blue, 3% grey). The attribution of 'virtual water' to Tony (J. A.) Allan (early 1990s; Stockholm Water Prize 2008) is corroborated by a WebSearch summary. Secondary source; definitions and figures reworded, and the beef figure flagged as a contested global average dominated by green water.

sourceRecords.title: Basic Information about Nonpoint Source (NPS) Pollution
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: the definition of nonpoint source pollution as any water pollution not meeting the Clean Water Act definition of a point source (a discrete conveyance such as a pipe or ditch); examples including excess fertilizers, herbicides, pesticides, sediment, salts, bacteria, and nutrients from farmland and urban runoff; and the statement that states report nonpoint source pollution as the leading remaining cause of water-quality problems. U.S. federal work; reworded originally.

sourceRecords.title: Sustainability of Ground-Water Resources (USGS Circular 1186)
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the source registry (same id and URL). Supports the intermediate renewable status of groundwater: recharge from precipitation replenishes it, but often at much smaller rates than withdrawals, so it is neither fully renewable like solar energy nor non-renewable like a petroleum deposit. U.S. federal work; reworded originally.
